analysis.one_liner: Requires the Interior Department to sell Gulf of Mexico oil and gas leases twice every year.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023, despite sponsorship by 8 Republican senators.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would force the Interior Department to hold at least two oil and gas lease sales in the Gulf of Mexico every year, covering all unrestricted areas, and to lease to the highest bidder. It would also cap environmental reviews at 365 days (or 180 days for a single combined review) and give the department 75 days to approve offshore drilling permits, with approval required unless there are clear grounds to deny. The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Offshore oil and gas producers, who would get a legal guarantee of two Gulf lease sales a year regardless of which administration is in office, plus faster permitting and shorter environmental reviews. Gulf state governments would also gain, because offshore lease sales generate federal revenue, part of which is shared with Gulf states under existing law.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Interior Department to hold at least two region-wide Gulf of Mexico lease sales per year, each including areas in both the Central and Western Gulf planning areas, beginning in fiscal 2022.
Requires each sale to include all unleased areas not subject to restrictions and leases to go to the highest responsible qualified bidder, taking away agency discretion over which parcels to offer.

Caps environmental reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act at less than 365 days for lease-by-lease reviews or 180 days for a single programmatic review, with a decision document required.
Gives the department 75 days to act on offshore exploration, development, and production permits, and requires approval 'absent clear grounds for denial,' shifting the default toward approval.

analysis.who_pays: Coastal communities, commercial and recreational fishing interests, and taxpayers bear the added environmental risk of legally mandated drilling in Gulf waters, including spill risk, because the bill mandates sales regardless of conditions and compresses the time available to study impacts and take public comment. Future administrations also lose the ability to slow or pause Gulf leasing for environmental or market reasons.

drawbacks.text: Mandating two lease sales every year regardless of environmental, safety, or market conditions removes the ability of elected administrations and agencies to adjust leasing to conditions in the Gulf, a region that experienced the Deepwater Horizon spill.
Environmental review deadlines of 365 or 180 days are shorter than many such reviews now take and limit the time for scientific analysis and public input on the risks of expanding offshore drilling.
The requirement to grant permits 'absent clear grounds for denial' within 75 days tilts the approval process toward industry and makes rejection the exception rather than a considered outcome.

An honest supporter would acknowledge the trade-off the bill's own title points to: offshore lease sales produce revenue, part of which funds conservation and Gulf state programs, and the bill's backers argued restricting sales threatens that funding. The cost is accelerated drilling and reduced environmental scrutiny in the same waters.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a clear, durable benefit to offshore oil and gas producers: guaranteed annual access to Gulf leases, faster permits, and shorter reviews. Its stated public rationale is protecting conservation funding that flows from lease revenue. But the public-side benefits are indirect and small compared with the costs: legally mandated drilling in Gulf waters with sharply compressed environmental review and a default-approve permitting standard. The design serves the industry's core asks first and treats environmental analysis as a deadline problem rather than a safety question.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee on January 27, 2021, and sat there without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote until the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Senator John Kennedy introduced the bill on January 27, 2021, with seven Republican cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day.
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no vote on the bill, and it never reached the Senate floor during the 117th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, Gulf waters were not placed under a legal mandate for two lease sales a year, and federal agencies kept their discretion over offshore leasing pace and environmental review. Gulf coastal and fishing interests were spared the mandated expansion; offshore producers remain under existing law rather than a guaranteed annual schedule.

for.name: Sen. John Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which mandates annual Gulf lease sales and speeded permitting.

for.name: 7 of 50 Senate Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors (Hyde-Smith, Cassidy, Cruz, Daines, Cornyn, Wicker, Lummis)

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; took no action
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, all from oil- and gas-producing states; no Democrat or independent joined, and no vote was ever held to test broader support.

industries.note: The bill guarantees producers two Gulf lease sales a year with all unrestricted acreage offered, caps environmental reviews at 365 or 180 days, and defaults permits to approval within 75 days. That is expanded, faster access to public waters at the public's environmental expense.

industries.industry: Offshore drilling and oilfield services contractors
industries.note: Mandated annual sales and 75-day permit deadlines translate into more rig and service work in the Gulf, the industry's direct customer base.

industries.industry: Gulf commercial fishing and coastal tourism
industries.note: More mandated drilling footprint and compressed review of spill and discharge risks fall on waters these industries depend on, so their interest runs with the broader public's.

Offshore lease sales generate federal revenue, a share of which flows to Gulf states and coastal political subdivisions under existing law, so more mandated sales mean more of that money; the bill's title reflects this conservation-funding rationale.
